questions.stem: A book rests on a table with no resultant force acting on it. According to Newton's First Law, what will happen to the book?

options.text: It will slowly start to move
It will remain at rest
It will vibrate on the spot
It will accelerate downward

questions.explanation: Newton's First Law states that an object at rest will remain at rest unless acted upon by a resultant force. Since the forces are balanced (weight downward equals the normal contact force upward), the book stays still. It does not need a force to 'keep it still' — the absence of a resultant force is sufficient.

questions.stem: A spacecraft is travelling at 5000 m/s in deep space, far from any gravitational fields. Its engines are switched off. What happens to its velocity?

options.text: It gradually slows down and stops
It continues at 5000 m/s in the same direction
It speeds up because there is no friction
It immediately stops

questions.explanation: Newton's First Law says a moving object continues at constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force. In deep space with no friction or gravity, there is no resultant force, so the spacecraft continues at 5000 m/s indefinitely. Option (a) reflects the common misconception that objects need a force to keep moving — they do not.

questions.stem: A car travels along a straight road at a constant velocity of 25 m/s. What can you conclude about the forces acting on the car?

options.text: The driving force is greater than the resistive forces
No forces are acting on the car
The resultant force on the car is zero
Only the driving force is acting on the car

questions.explanation: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, which by Newton's First Law means the resultant force is zero. The driving force exactly balances all resistive forces (friction, air resistance). Option (b) is wrong — forces are acting, but they are balanced. Option (a) would cause acceleration, not constant velocity.

questions.stem: When a bus brakes suddenly, passengers lurch forward. Which concept from Newton's First Law explains this?

options.text: Gravity pulls passengers forward
The bus pushes passengers forward
Inertia — passengers' bodies tend to continue moving at the original speed
Air resistance pushes passengers forward

questions.explanation: Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist changes in its motion. When the bus brakes, the braking force acts on the bus, but the passengers' bodies tend to continue at the original speed (Newton's First Law). They lurch forward relative to the bus because their inertia keeps them moving. This is why seatbelts are essential.

questions.stem: A skydiver falls at a constant terminal velocity of 55 m/s. What is the resultant force acting on the skydiver?

options.text: Equal to their weight
Greater than their weight
0 N

questions.explanation: At terminal velocity, speed is constant, meaning acceleration is zero. By Newton's First Law, this means the resultant force is zero — air resistance exactly equals the skydiver's weight. Option (a) is only true if air resistance were zero. Option (d) confuses velocity with force. At terminal velocity: weight = drag, so resultant = 0.
